title: Waiting for CT in the hallway
objective: Recognize rising intracranial pressure from a falling level of consciousness, then pupil changes and Cushing's triad

brief.situation: 23:10 in a crowded emergency department. You are the nurse for the hallway beds. Mr. Doyle, 44, fell from a bar stool at 22:30 and struck his head on the floor. He smells of beer. He is in a hallway bed waiting for a head CT; the scanner is backed up about 40 minutes.
handover: Triage: GCS 14 (confused to time), pupils 3 mm and equal, blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 88. A scalp hematoma over the right temple. No blood thinners.
The physician's orders: head CT when the scanner is free, neuro checks every hour, nothing by mouth.
The physician is in the department and wants to hear about any change. Department practice: a drop of 2 or more GCS points is reported at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Check him as often as you think he needs; each check takes a minute. The order says hourly; you decide whether that is enough.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: An expanding hematoma raises the pressure over about 35 minutes. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Head of the bed at 30 degrees with the neck midline slows the rise a little. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of a dilating right pupil. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of Cushing's triad. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of herniation. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A GCS drop of 2 or more reported within 5 minutes (department practice).
The first neuro check within 5 minutes of taking over (department practice).
A stat CT and the neurosurgeon: about 10 min to leave the department.

why.question: Mr. Doyle is drowsier. Is it the beer? What do you do?

parts.label: What it means
parts.criteria: A falling GCS with worsening headache and vomiting after a head strike is rising intracranial pressure, the earliest sign; pupil changes and Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) are late signs of herniation; alcohol is not the explanation for a falling GCS.
parts.modelAnswer: His GCS is falling, his headache is worse and he is vomiting after a blow to the head. That is rising intracranial pressure, and the falling level of consciousness is the earliest sign. Three beers don't explain a dropping GCS. A blown pupil and Cushing's triad would be late.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Neuro checks far more often than hourly; reports a 2-point drop at once for a stat CT and neurosurgery; head of the bed at 30 degrees, neck midline.
parts.modelAnswer: I check him every few minutes, not hourly, tell the physician now for a stat CT and neurosurgery, and raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees with his neck midline.

noProgress.rationale: A falling level of consciousness after head injury still unscanned an hour on is harm here.

Check again: still GCS 14. Ask his friend: vomiting, three beers.
GCS 12 with worse headache: the earliest sign. Tell the physician now: stat CT.
Hand off the GCS trend with times.

herniation.headline: Herniation
herniation.body: A falling GCS after a head strike is the earliest sign of rising pressure; a blown pupil and Cushing's triad are late. Never put it down to alcohol.

earlyCt.headline: Caught early
earlyCt.body: Frequent checks found the falling GCS, and you reported it before any pupil change. That is the expert path.

lateCt.headline: Scanned on late signs
lateCt.body: Check how often you looked, how long the drop waited for a report, and whether a pupil had already changed.

time_up.headline: Still in the hallway
time_up.body: A falling GCS after head injury needs a scan within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: After a head strike, a GCS that falls from 14 to 12 with worsening headache and vomiting is rising intracranial pressure; the level of consciousness is the earliest sign, and pupil changes and Cushing's triad of hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing are late signs of herniation. A few beers don't explain it. Hourly checks are too slow: check every few minutes, report a 2-point drop at once for a stat CT and neurosurgery, and keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees with the neck midline.

earlyQ.ask: While you assess: which is the earliest sign of rising intracranial pressure?
earlyQ.explain: Altered mental status from drowsiness to coma comes first; Cushing triad is a late and ominous sign of impending herniation.

triadQ.ask: While he goes to CT: what makes up Cushing's triad?
triadQ.explain: Cushing triad is hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration, a late sign of impending herniation.
